points.question: Chilean fruit is on hold with Customs. What do you do?

options.text: Keep the hold on all Chilean fruit until inspectors have sampled it.
Judge the threat a hoax and ask Customs to release the fruit.
Keep the hold and wait to see whether the caller rings again.
Warn the public and the other importing countries that the fruit may be poisoned.

before.q: FDA inspectors: by 12 March they had examined about 1,200 of some 365,000 crates on the Almeria Star and analyzed about 75 suspicious samples.

points.question: Your Philadelphia laboratory has found cyanide in two grapes. What do you do?

options.text: Retest what is left of the sample at a second laboratory before acting.
Hold the Almeria Star's cargo only, and go on inspecting.
Suspend imports of Chilean fruit and notify the other importing countries.
Treat the two grapes as an isolated tampering and say so publicly.

did_q.q: Imports of Chilean fruit were suspended from 13 to 17 March.
The FDA: notified other importing countries, including Canada and Japan.

then.q: The FDA's Cincinnati laboratory: a later analysis, which fell below its detection limit.

before.q: The General Accounting Office: reviewed the file at Senator Jesse Helms's request.

options.text: That a result on two grapes was too slight to justify suspending a country's exports.
That no conclusion is possible without the Chilean exporters' own supply-chain records.
That the tests and the chain of custody hold up, and the FDA acted properly.

did_q.q: reported on 6 September 1990 that both tests were widely used and accepted, that it found no serious deficiencies in the chain of custody, and that its consultants considered a false positive extremely unlikely.

then.q: No perpetrator was identified; the caller had said his purpose was to draw attention to the poor living conditions of Chilean workers.
